0 to 1Every build from scratch

Trojan horse, step by step

Step 1

Concept sketch

It starts in a notebook. The Trojan Horse is drawn as a triangulated lattice: a rearing pose broken into straight members a steel frame can follow. Notes mark repeated parts (2x) and a weight at the base so it will not tip.

Step 2

Dimensioned drawing

Side and back views with real numbers: 30°, 51°, 54° and 65° member angles, a 4.2 ft base, and a wire structure for the ribs. This drawing decides every cut length.

Step 3

Source the material

Thin rods for ribs and mane, square tube and strip for the skeleton. Sourced from workshop scrap and offcuts, then measured against the drawing.

Step 4

Mark and cut

Pieces are laid out full size on the floor and labelled in chalk ("cut", "lower leg"), so the layout can be checked before any welding.

Step 5

De-rust and sand

Rusty bars are wire-brushed and sanded by hand so the welds bite into clean steel.

Step 6

Weld the frame

Members are tacked and welded on an X-shaped base. The triangles give stiffness: the frame carries the horse before any skin is added.

Step 7

Skin and ribs

Cardboard, newspaper and tape are layered over the steel to make the body, with the rib bands following the wire structure from the drawing.

Step 8

The finished horse

Standing about 10 ft tall, built by a team in the studio over long nights.

Dragon, step by step

Step 1

Sketch and scale

The dragon begins as a folded paper strip sketch beside a human figure for scale, then a whiteboard structure plan with the main dimensions.

Step 2

Scrap sourcing

Pallets, pipes, old tyres, hoses and mesh from around campus become the raw material.

Step 3

Frame and layers

A wooden frame is wrapped in cardboard, newspaper and tape to form the head and the long body.

Step 4

Paint and finish

Painted red and black with horns, teeth and an open walk-in mouth. About 20 ft long and 8 to 9 ft tall.

Thinking of engineering?

A starting map for school students and first-years who want to explore mechanical and other branches.

What mechanical covers

  • Statics and strength of materials: why things stand or break
  • Thermodynamics and fluids: engines, pumps, cooling
  • Machine design: gears, shafts, bearings, linkages
  • Manufacturing: cutting, welding, casting, 3D printing

Tools to learn first

  • Fusion 360 or SolidWorks for 3D design
  • Python for calculations and data
  • Arduino for sensors, motors and control
  • A notebook: sketch before you model

Three projects for this week

  • Build a cardboard bridge and load-test it with books
  • Model and 3D print a pair of meshing gears
  • Make an Arduino robot that stops before it hits a wall

Branches at a glance

  • Mechanical: machines, motion, energy, making things
  • Civil: buildings, bridges, roads, water
  • Electrical: circuits, power, motors, electronics
  • Computer: software, data, AI. Many projects mix all four
